planting.note: Prune as Group 2 (or hard back in late winter if grown as Group 3) since it blooms on new wood over an unusually long season. Can also be planted in fall.

directions: A hybrid of the fargesii/potaninii group also sold under the trade name Summer Snow, this exceptionally vigorous climber smothers itself in small, single, fragrant white flowers with cream stamens from midsummer clear into early autumn, far outlasting the single spring or early-summer flush of most large-flowered hybrids. New growth is purplish-bronze before maturing to green, and the sheer bloom quantity plus long season make it a favorite for covering a large arbor, fence, or unsightly structure quickly. Unlike the montana types it does not require pruning restraint tied to old wood, giving gardeners more flexibility in shaping it.

planting.note: Pruning group 2; light pruning after the first flush encourages a strong repeat bloom. Can also be planted in fall.

directions: Raised by the Jackman nursery in 1871 and named for a mistress of Henry II, this large-flowered heirloom bears bluish-white blooms 4 to 6 inches across marked with a soft red bar and a bold cluster of purple stamens. It is one of the more reliably fragrant large-flowered clematis, a trait many modern hybrids lack, and the pale coloring holds truest with a little afternoon shade. Two distinct flushes appear each season, an early one on old wood and a second on new growth in late summer, giving a longer season of interest than single-flush hybrids like Jackmanii.

planting.note: Pruning group 2; the semi-double early flowers form on old wood, so limit cutting back to just after the first flush. Can also be planted in fall.

directions: An 1873 Jackman-raised hybrid of 'Candida' and 'Fortunei', this compact climber opens broad, overlapping creamy-white sepals in a semi-double form up to 7 inches wide during its late spring flush, with pinkish-brown stamens at the center. A second wave of single, slightly smaller white flowers follows in late summer and autumn. Its restrained size relative to vigorous Jackman-group siblings like Jackmanii Superba suits a small fence, obelisk, or container rather than a large wall.

planting.note: Non-climbing herbaceous type; cut stems back hard after flowering to refresh the purple foliage color and control sprawl.

directions: Unlike the vining hybrids and species, this non-climbing selection of the herbaceous species Clematis recta is grown chiefly for its foliage, which emerges deep burgundy-purple in spring and gradually fades toward grey-green as the season progresses. In early summer it sends up airy clusters of small, star-shaped, vanilla-scented white flowers held well above the foliage, followed by silvery seedheads. Left unsupported it sprawls and scrambles through neighboring plants rather than climbing, so it works best staked or allowed to lean into a border companion.

planting.note: Pruning group 2; tolerates partial and even bright north-facing shade better than most large-flowered hybrids while still flowering heavily. Can also be planted in fall.

directions: Bred by Polish Jesuit monk Brother Stefan Franczak and named for Pope John Paul II, this large-flowered hybrid produces luminous creamy-white blooms 5 to 6 inches across with a faint soft pink central stripe on each sepal and a prominent tuft of red stamens. It flowers in two distinct waves, first from late spring into midsummer and again in early fall, giving a longer display than single-flush cultivars such as Henryi. Its unusual tolerance for shadier exposures, including north-facing walls, makes it a practical choice where other large-flowered clematis would bloom poorly.

planting.note: Herbaceous scrambling type that blooms on new wood; cut hard back to the ground in late winter like a Group 3 clematis. Can also be planted in fall.

directions: Discovered as a chance seedling of Clematis tubulosa and C. virginiana in a Cleveland, Ohio garden in the 1930s, this scrambling herbaceous hybrid behaves more like a sprawling sub-shrub than a true climber and benefits from a low trellis or the support of neighboring shrubs. In late summer it produces hundreds of small, faintly fragrant, pale bluish-white flowers with recurved, slightly twisted sepals and prominent creamy stamens, giving a hazy cloud effect distinct from the large single blooms of hybrids like Jackmanii. Its late-season bloom and non-climbing habit make it a useful filler at the front of a mixed border rather than on an arbor.
